TextView.android:text: Intermediate Lesson 15: Radical Axis & Isogonal Conjugates

Recall the Power of a Point. The Radical Axis of two circles is the straight line consisting of all points that have the EXACT SAME power with respect to both circles. If the circles intersect, their radical axis is simply the line passing through their intersection points.\nMore importantly, if you have THREE circles, their three radical axes intersect at a single concurrent point called the Radical Center. This is a brilliant tool to prove that three lines intersect at one point without using Ceva's theorem.

If you take a Cevian (a line from a vertex) and reflect it across the angle bisector of that vertex, you get its isogonal line. \nIf three Cevians intersect at a point P, their three isogonal reflections will also intersect at a single point P'. P and P' are called Isogonal Conjugates.\nThe most famous pair of Isogonal Conjugates in a triangle are the Orthocenter (H) and the Circumcenter (O)! Another famous pair is the Centroid (G) and the Lemoine Point.

Often known as 'Fact 5' in Olympiad folklore, this lemma is incredibly powerful. 
Let I be the incenter of triangle ABC, and let the angle bisector of A intersect the circumcircle at point M. 
The lemma states that M is the center of a circle that passes through B, I, C, and the A-excenter! 
This means MB = MI = MC = M(Excenter). This instantly gives you isosceles triangles and equal segments to work with.

We know Ptolemy's Theorem applies to cyclic quadrilaterals. But what if the quadrilateral is NOT cyclic?
Ptolemy's Inequality states that for ANY four points A, B, C, D in a plane: 
AB * CD + BC * AD ≥ AC * BD.
Equality holds if and only if ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with the vertices in that specific order. This is heavily used in geometry optimization problems to find minimum distances.
In triangle ABC, the angle bisector of A meets the circumcircle at M. If the distance from M to vertex B is 7, what is the distance from M to the incenter I of the triangle?

Solution: By the Incenter-Excenter Lemma (Fact 5), the intersection of the angle bisector with the circumcircle (Point M) acts as the center of a circle passing through B, C, and the incenter I. \nTherefore, the distances from M to B, M to C, and M to I are all radii of this same circle and must be exactly equal. \nSince MB = 7, then MI = 7.

Circles X, Y, and Z intersect such that the common chord of X and Y is line L1, and the common chord of Y and Z is line L2. If L1 and L2 intersect at a point P, what is the power of point P with respect to circle Z relative to its power to circle X?

Solution: The common chord of two intersecting circles is exactly their Radical Axis. 
Since P lies on L1 (the radical axis of X and Y), Power(P, X) = Power(P, Y). 
Since P also lies on L2 (the radical axis of Y and Z), Power(P, Y) = Power(P, Z). 
By transitivity, Power(P, X) = Power(P, Z). Point P is the Radical Center of the three circles, so its power with respect to all three circles is identical.
